name: Toto
lead: Toto is a Critically Endangered Sino-Tibetan (Tibeto-Burman) language spoken in the village of Totopara in Alipurduar district, West Bengal, along the India–Bhutan border.[1][2] Within Tibeto-Burman, George van Driem classifies Toto alongside Dhimal in the Dhimalish subgroup.[2]
history:
The Toto community resides in a single geographical enclave, Totopara, bordered by the Torsha River to the east and the foothills of Bhutan to the north.[1] Fieldwork by Amitabha Sengupta and Basanta Kumar Roy and later by George van Driem documented the grammar and lexicon.[1][2]

In 2015, community elder and writer Dhaniram Toto developed an indigenous 31-letter alphabet for the language, which was encoded in The Unicode Standard (Version 14.0, block U+1E290–U+1E2BF) in 2021.[4] Despite community literacy initiatives, multi-lingual contact with Nepali and Bengali in Totopara has led to language shift among younger speakers.[3]
phonology: Toto possesses six oral vowels (/i, e, ə, a, o, u/) and a phonemic glottal stop /ʔ/.[1][2] Its consonant inventory contrasts voiceless unaspirated, voiceless aspirated, and voiced stops across bilabial, dental/alveolar, palatal, and velar places of articulation, plus a series of voiced and voiceless nasals and liquids.[2]
syntax: Toto is verb-final (SOV). Nominal case relations are marked by enclitic postpositions: ergative/instrumental -nā, dative/accusative -kē, genitive -kō, and locative -tā.[1][2]
